text: Architecture meeting. Redis was proposed for distributed coordination because it could provide low-latency lock operations. The team agreed to ask Operations whether adding another stateful service was justified before making the choice.
title: Project Orchid locking design

text: Operations review. The team already operates Postgres with established backup, patching, monitoring, and on-call procedures. Adding Redis would introduce another stateful service, failure mode, patch cycle, and operational ownership burden. Recommendation: avoid Redis unless measured requirements cannot be met with the existing Postgres platform.
title: Operations review of Redis option

author: lead@orchid.example
text: Decision for the first release: do not add Redis. Use Postgres advisory locks. The reason is operational complexity and the cost of owning another stateful service, not a belief that Redis is technically poor. Revisit only if measurements show the Postgres approach is insufficient.
title: Orchid first-release coordination decision

text: Performance note. A synthetic burst at roughly twenty times the expected first-release load showed advisory-lock contention. This test is intentionally unrealistic for current traffic. The next action is profiling and realistic load measurement. This note does not reverse the no-Redis decision.
title: Lock contention burst test

text: INC-77 update at 09:12. Database CPU is saturated and request latency is rising. Initial working hypothesis: database capacity may be the cause. This is an early hypothesis and is not confirmed.
title: INC-77 initial observation

text: INC-77 update at 09:25. Retry volume and queue depth increased sharply after the timeout configuration rollout. Pausing retries caused database CPU to fall. The team began rolling back the timeout configuration.
title: INC-77 retry signal

text: INC-77 postmortem. Root cause: the timeout configuration rollout caused a retry storm. Database CPU saturation was a downstream symptom, not the initiating cause. This final assessment supersedes the early database-capacity hypothesis. The incident began at 09:12 according to the corrected event record.
title: INC-77 postmortem

text: INC-77 addendum. The previously circulated timeline listed 09:10 as the start time; the source log shows the incident began at 09:12. Correct the start time to 09:12. The root-cause assessment remains the retry storm triggered by the timeout configuration rollout.
title: INC-77 timing correction

text: Legal memo for customer Cobalt. Production customer data must remain in the European Union. The same residency restriction applies to subprocessors handling that production data.
title: Cobalt residency requirement

text: Procurement meeting. Cobalt repeated the EU data-residency requirement and specifically asked where disaster-recovery copies would be stored. Northstar could not confirm during the meeting that the standard disaster-recovery configuration keeps every copy in the EU.
title: Cobalt procurement discussion

author: security@cobalt.example
text: Cobalt clarification: the EU-only requirement includes backups and replicas, not just primary storage. A backup outside the EU is non-compliant unless the contract is amended.
title: Cobalt clarification on backups

text: Northstar response. Primary storage can be located in the EU. Under the standard disaster-recovery configuration, encrypted backups may be stored in the United States. Northstar also offers an EU-only disaster-recovery option, but it is not the default configuration.
title: Northstar disaster-recovery options
